items.title: A Professional Smile
items.content:
You are a gossip columnist who ghost-wrote Vale's autobiography, so you know his dirt. Tonight you circulate with your Polaroid camera, taking candid frames and writing the time on the ones worth timing. Nobody sees a print until you are sure those times are right.

Between pictures, find Sabrina Sinclair, the tabloid journalist, Brenda Blip, the Radio 1 DJ, and Chuck Chambers, the talk-show host, and swap what you each know about Vale.

items.title: The Reception Pictures
items.content:
You photographed the reception: greetings, a dance, a group conversation, portraits, the champagne service and a signing in the lobby. Those ordinary scenes show people socialising, not the contents of a recording or interference with the decanter. Nobody sees a print until you have checked the times written on them: a doubtful time could start a false accusation.

Agent 'Rosemary' watched the room as closely as your camera did. Ask her what she was looking for.

items.title: The Last Clear Frame
items.content:
Your decanter photograph was taken at 19:29:10 on 10 October 1986; you noted the cue-clock time after the exposure. The frame shows a woman from behind, her hand near the stopper, not powder entering the wine. Every table has been holding that picture since the last round without knowing what it was.

Show it to Nikki Neon first and ask whether she recognises the woman from her own view. Then tell the tables which picture it is, and what the time on it means.

items.title: Vale’s Private Card — Arrival and Toast
items.content:
GM TO VALE — Your private card, handed over at arrival. It covers all of Round 0.

You are the host everybody came to see. Welcome guests warmly and enjoy a posh red from your private decanter. Marianne Moonbeam, the healer, will peer into your aura and offer a playful reading of your future. You have heard her misty warnings before: laugh it off.

**After 7:30 pm:** at the toast, welcome everyone to tonight's gala, but wait for the single twenty-second music and stage-light cue to subside. Drink from the private decanter and stage the collapse at the rehearsed cue. No substance is added to a real drink.

Then leave discreetly to return as Peter in Round 1, stating your fictional arrival time of 19:55 from your Round 1 card.

items.title: An Easier Technical Conversation
items.content:
You are a Brummie IT consultant obsessed with microchips, and you know more than you say. You secretly copied Vale's files, and you know what is on the tape he has been holding. The thought of it surfacing makes your stomach tighten.

Find Peter Packard, the technology investor, and Barry Byte, the ByteCorp salesman, and talk about networks and new ideas. Technical talk is easier than explaining what you know about somebody else's recordings.

items.title: The File Behind Comeback Girl
items.content:
Your copied BBC recording names Vale and Veronica. He claims half her performance fees; she admits signing his management agreement at eighteen. Vale's attached publicity note identifies her new lead role in a BBC period drama. You copied it before the gala, so it contains no footage of tonight.

After a death, keeping quiet about the threat to Veronica feels worse than admitting you took the copy. Compare its contents with Brenda Blip's memory of the studio.

items.title: The Cue Desk
items.content:
You heard a two-second microphone crackle from the technical desk as the loud music started, and saw the same cue clock as Peter Packard. Last week you copied a file labelled Comeback Girl, scheduled after the toast. You are keeping its contents to yourself: telling would expose your theft.

Ask Peter Packard, the tech investor, where he was when he heard the crackle and what he could see.

items.title: What the Music Was Paid to Do
items.content:
You copied the BBC exchange before this gala: Vale claims half Veronica's performance fees and she admits signing his agreement. The attached publicity note names her new BBC period-drama role. That gives the unplayed recording a human cost beyond a technical failure.

Tell DJ Spinny T what it contained and ask what the anonymous music instruction paid him to do.

items.title: A Discreet Introduction
items.content:
You were once a GCHQ technician, and you got out, or tried to. Then Vale drew you into his systems, and you have never been sure whether he knew about your past or was using it. Tonight you trust almost nobody.

Find Mandy Modem, the hacker-for-hire, and Colin Cable, the network engineer, and ask about their work. Keep your own past vague until you know how much they like talking about other people's secrets.

items.title: Inside the Archive
items.content:
Your old intelligence connections made you fear what Vale might have kept in his archive. You worked around his systems, but never inspected every file. Not knowing is almost worse than knowing.

Find Mandy Modem and ask whether she entered the archive and what she found there.

items.title: The Unplayed Recording
items.content:
You understand how an insecure archive could let someone read private material. You still want to know why the recording intended for the toast never played.

Ask Colin Cable what controlled the playback and what he found when he checked it after the collapse.

items.title: The Cost of a Secret
items.content:
Vale is dead, the archive is still there, and you will never now find out whether your intelligence past was in it. You will have to live as though it was.

Lady Helena de Brissac has lived with the same kind of threat. Ask her what Vale could have said about her name.

items.title: The Cost of Your Image
items.content:
You used church donations to cover gambling debts, and Vale had the records. He also knew you were married to Lola. You left the main room for a private conversation together, but are not ready to name your companion or discuss the marriage.

Vale kept a file on Crystal DeVille too. Ask her what he held over her reputation.

items.title: A Familiar Face
items.content:
You are a televangelist with a carefully managed image. You used church donations to cover gambling debts, and you are secretly married to Lola Lasalle. Vale knows both and planned to expose them together; your ministry would not survive it.

Find Lola Lasalle and Crystal DeVille, the showbiz agent. Greet Lola warmly enough to look natural, and no more. Crystal will want to know how you manage the press.

items.title: Say Her Name
items.content:
You were with Lola in the conservatory before the music began and stayed there until after the collapse. She is your wife. You concealed the marriage to protect your ministry, but secrecy now risks making a private conversation look like involvement in a killing.

Tell Crystal DeVille about the marriage, then ask what she saw from the balcony.

items.title: Behind the Conservatory Door
items.content:
You and Lola stayed in the conservatory from before the music until after the collapse, talking about whether to acknowledge your marriage. You are still keeping her name private.

Roxie Runway, the model, has the look of someone hiding a relationship, and you know that look. Ask her what Vale could expose about her.

items.title: A Confident Comeback
items.content:
You are a former soap star making a comeback: you have just signed to lead a new BBC period drama. At eighteen you signed Vale's perpetual management contract, giving him half of every performance fee. Tonight he plans to 'congratulate' you at the toast by playing a hot-mic tape of you admitting it. You cannot let it play. Your gown is a Fiona Fringe design.

Scooter will hand you a sealed compact in secret: Beverly's sample, for Vale. While DJ Spinny T causes a distraction, set it unseen on the private drinks table beside Vale's decanter. Then find Angie Vixen, Lucien Luxe and Fiona Fringe.

items.title: The Price of a Comeback
items.content:
You have signed to lead a new BBC period drama. At eighteen you signed Vale's management agreement giving him half your performance fees, and have never escaped it. Public exposure of that existing claim could frighten your new employer and wreck the comeback. His promised recording contains your admission of signing.

Ask Lola Lasalle what Vale had on her, and whether she ever stopped expecting him to use it.

items.title: The Compact and the Wine
items.content:
You accepted the compact for Vale's inspection. When you requested it, Beverly made a point of saying it was an undiluted multi-dose sample rather than a finished dose.

Read the laboratory report on your table, then find Inspector Donna Reed and ask whether it shows who put the stimulant in the wine. Hear her answer before deciding what it means.
items.footnote: ON YOUR TABLE · The laboratory report, handed to your table by Inspector Donna Reed · SHARED

items.title: The Sample You Accepted
items.content:
Scooter brought you a sealed silver compact for Vale to inspect. You would like to understand the sample you accepted.

Beverly makes the ingredient for Graham Greenwell's new wellness remedy, as he has been telling anyone who will listen. Ask him how the ingredient was meant to be used.

items.title: The Promised Scoop
items.content:
You recently interviewed Vale for BBC Radio 1. After the official end, the microphone stayed live and caught Vale and Veronica Vane discussing her management contract. Vale kept the cassette, and has promised to give you back your scoop by playing it at the toast.

Find Sabrina Sinclair, the tabloid journalist, Chuck Chambers and Vance Vellum. Talk shop, and ask Sabrina why she has brought a notebook. Do not give away your exclusive.

items.title: A Toast Interrupted
items.content:
Vale told you he would play your BBC recording after the toast as a congratulation for Veronica. You expected a scoop; instead, he collapsed.

Whatever stopped your scoop happened in the twenty seconds before the toast, and Leo Lights ran them. Ask him how the music and lights were timed.

items.title: A Scoop Turned Into a Weapon
items.content:
You heard it yourself in the BBC studio: Vale claiming half of Veronica's performance fees, and Veronica admitting she signed the agreement. Vale later promised to play that tape after the toast, calling it a congratulation.

Tell Inspector Donna Reed exactly what you heard. Your scoop matters less now than helping her understand what that tape meant to the people on it.

items.title: What You Heard Live
items.content:
You heard Vale state that he took half Veronica's performance fees, and heard her admit signing the agreement. He promised to play it after the toast. You wanted your scoop back; hearing her career discussed as his property felt different.

Find Veronica Vane, tell her what you heard in the studio, and ask why the recording threatened her new BBC role.

items.title: What Does the Inspector Know?
items.content:
The separate dish you prepared was intended for Vale. You added a non-lethal sedative to make him too drowsy to give his speech, fearing exposure of your prescribing. It was withdrawn before service.

When Veronica requested the compact, you warned her that the undiluted sample could be fatal if swallowed whole. She said Vale only wanted to inspect it.

Read the laboratory report on your table, then find Inspector Donna Reed and ask what she makes of what it found in the separate dish. Hear how much she knows before you decide how much to say.
items.footnote: ON YOUR TABLE · The laboratory report, handed to your table by Inspector Donna Reed · SHARED

items.title: A Discreet Favour
items.content:
Vale knows too much about you. You prescribe his stimulants, and you supply an ingredient to Cherry Bomb Wellness. Ronnie Reels and Graham Greenwell are your clients too.

In a panic, you put a non-lethal sedative in Vale's separate dish, to make him too drowsy for his speech.

You also sent Veronica a sealed silver compact, supposedly for Vale to inspect. Scooter carried it: she quietly carries all your deliveries.

Find Cassie Chase, Dakota Steele and Inspector Donna Reed. Cassie has been fussing over the special service: ask her, lightly, whether Vale's dish will reach him.

items.title: A Sign Is Not a Diagnosis
items.content:
You supplied Vale with stimulants before the gala. His earlier sharpness was familiar, but his appearance alone cannot tell you the dose or why he collapsed. At least the dish never reached him: Cassie had it withdrawn, and so far nobody knows what you put in it.

Ask Cassie Chase what she saw before his final drink, and whether she saw the earlier symptoms begin.

items.title: The Undiluted Sample
items.content:
You sealed an undiluted multi-dose formulation sample in the silver compact marked VV. Veronica said Vale wanted to inspect it; Scooter carried it to her. You expected it back unopened. After the service check, you stayed with Cassie at the hatch through the music and alarm.

Explain the sample to Graham Greenwell and ask what he has been telling investors the remedy contains.

items.title: A Gracious Introduction
items.content:
You lead a televangelist ministry, and you are a fake: the title is not yours. You built 'Lady Helena de Brissac' and the aristocratic past that goes with it, and it has given your ministry a respectability no preaching could buy. Vale knows, and could end your marriage and your ministry with one sentence about where the name came from.

Find Cassette Carl, Sasha Smirnoff and Wendy Woke. People who trade recordings know the cost of a reputation.

items.title: A Question of Dress
items.content:
You saw a covered dish returning towards service, but did not inspect it or read its label. Your fear of what Vale could say about the name gave you reason to watch the room.

Ask Fiona Fringe what she found in the hem of the gown she designed. You notice how people are dressed; she saw something on this dress after the toast.

items.title: What Came Back from Service
items.content:
You saw the covered dish taken back towards the hatch, but did not read the label or inspect its contents. It is frustrating to have noticed something without knowing what it means.

Ask Cassie Chase whose dish was withdrawn and why. A carefully kept history has made you attentive to arrangements other people overlook.

items.title: What You Left Behind
items.content:
Vale could end your ministry by revealing what you left behind when you took the name: an affair with a servant in the house where you once worked.

Years in that house taught you what it means when a dinner is sent back. Tonight you saw a covered dish carried back towards the service hatch, where Cassie Chase looked cross and Dr. Beverly Steele looked worse. You did not read its label or inspect it.

Ask Dr. Beverly Steele why it came back.

items.title: Two Early Crashes
items.content:
You heard backstage damage around 19:20–19:21, well before the later music cue. You would know that temper anywhere: Rex 'Razor' Steele got the career Vale promised you, then smashed it the way he smashes everything. Smile. Breathe. Establish what broke before every crash becomes the same incident.

Ask Rex 'Razor' Steele what he damaged and when, and keep your voice level while he answers.

items.title: A Passing Encounter
items.content:
You saw Ricky outside the main-room doors during the cue, but it was a passing encounter. You also saw Rex below the guardrail on passes at 19:28:50 and 19:29:05, then stayed there until the alarm.

Tell Ricky Blaze when you noticed him outside. You can help with what you saw, without pretending to have watched the whole doorway interval.

items.title: The Gap Between Your Passes
items.content:
You saw Rex below the guardrail at 19:28:50, passed again at 19:29:05, and then stayed until the alarm. Between those passes you were looking elsewhere. You cannot account for every second.

Vale gave Rex the career that should have been yours. You have kept your temper all these years; you will not lose it now, for Rex or against him.

Tell Rex 'Razor' Steele, the rock star, exactly what you can support.

items.title: A Lighter Conversation
items.content:
You are a lounge singer, all smiles. Years ago Vale signed you as a rock singer, then shelved you and pushed Rex 'Razor' Steele instead: the louder man, not the better voice. Rex threw it away in tantrums. You are far angrier than anyone here would guess; the easy charm is how you keep it down. Just.

Find Ricky Blaze, the stuntman and club owner, and Marshall 'Macho' Monroe, and talk about the old show-business crowd.

items.title: A Song Worth Playing
items.content:
You are a backup synth-pop singer, bright and eager on the surface. Nobody remembers the backup, which is why you get away with more than people expect. Vale promised you a record deal, then ghosted you, and you hate him for it.

Find DJ Spinny T, Leo Lights, the gaffer, and Scooter, the backstage messenger. Charm them into giving your songs the full treatment: recognition, volume and a little revenge.

items.title: Words in the Crowd
items.content:
Before the toast, you heard “He keeps everything” and “Not in here” from voices in the crowd. You could not reliably identify the speakers. Your own anger is clearer: Vale promised a record deal, then disappeared.

Tell Tina 'Tank' Thatcher, the Yorkshire activist, the words and ask why private recordings can give someone so much control.

items.title: The Passport Beneath the Sofa
items.content:
Helping Vance retrieve a dropped envelope of photographs beside the sofa, you found an old passport under a loose cushion. It carried Tina 'Tank' Thatcher's photograph and the name Patricia Margaret Thatcher. You did not see how it got there.

Describe the discovery to Tina 'Tank' Thatcher, the Yorkshire activist, and ask her to explain the name.
items.footnote: IN YOUR ENVELOPE · Item D: passport in Tina's former identity · PRIVATE

items.title: The Face Beside the Decanter
items.content:
From beside the west-side sofa, you recognised Veronica's face as she approached the private decanter during the music. You knew the gown and saw her clearly, but other guests blocked your view of her hands. That is the woman you can recognise in Vance's decanter picture.

You want to be taken seriously now. Tell Ronnie Reels, the filmmaker, what you saw and ask how much his camera position let him see.

items.title: The Material Behind the Machinery
items.content:
Vale cost you thousands but gave you no password, key or permission to read his private files. Your one useful observation remains the short microphone crackle.

Ask Tommy Tech what was on the recording he copied. You came looking for backing for a network that would connect everyone; you are beginning to see what Vale did with the one he had.

items.title: An Idea Worth Backing
items.content:
You are an early tech investor: nervous, analytical and desperate to get ahead of the curve. You lost thousands backing Vale's tech dream, and you need it back. Your own idea is a personal computer network you call the interweb. Most people do not get it yet.

Find Tommy Tech, the computer consultant, and Barry Byte, the ByteCorp salesman, and pitch them the interweb. They may see what a network connecting everyone would be worth.

items.title: At the Buffet Microphone
items.content:
You were testing a microphone connection beside the buffet when a brief crackle sounded at the start of the loud music. You were several paces from the private decanter and could not see all the hands around it. Vale's failed venture cost you thousands, but your investment gave you no archive access.

Ask Tommy Tech whether he heard the crackle from his technical position.

items.title: Two Seconds of Interference
items.content:
The microphone crackle lasted about two seconds at the start of the twenty-second music rise. You heard it beside the buffet and saw the cue clock. That does not tell you who caused every earlier disturbance backstage.

Ask Roxy Riot, the punk singer, when she broke her guitar. You want to separate a performer's outburst from the later sound fault.

items.title: Keeping the Camera Steady
items.content:
Beverly supplied individual stimulant doses for your work. Lately they felt stronger and less controlled. Vale knew about your dependency and threatened exposure unless you accepted his filming demands. From your east-wall camera position, people moving past repeatedly blocked your view of hands by the decanter.

Ask Tina Tanktop, the aerobics instructor, what she noticed about your behaviour.

items.title: Across the Room
items.content:
From your east-wall camera position, you recognised Veronica's profile beside the private decanter during the music. Her hand was near the stopper; then a passing guest blocked your view. You did not see a complete transfer into the wine.

Fear of exposing your dependency kept you quiet. The gown is the one detail you saw clearly, and Fiona Fringe designed it: tell Fiona whom you saw, and ask what she noticed about that gown.

items.title: Keeping Up With Work
items.content:
You are an indie filmmaker who notices the visual details others miss. Dr. Beverly Steele supplies the stimulants that keep you going through relentless deadlines, and lately the doses feel stronger and less controlled. Vale knows about your dependency and has hinted he will expose it unless you go along with his filming demands.

Find Tina Tanktop, the aerobics guru, Marianne Moonbeam and Roxie Runway, and talk about staying fit for long working days. Keep your hands still.

items.title: A Dose and a Sample
items.content:
You received individual doses from Beverly, not the sealed compact Scooter carried. From your east-wall camera position, the crowd turning towards the stage briefly opened your view of the private drinks area.

Ask Dr. Beverly Steele, the Harley Street doctor, whether the compact held a ready-to-take dose or a sample intended to be diluted.

items.title: An Ordinary Conversation
items.content:
You are an off-duty CID officer, sidelined by an internal probe into a two-year-old conviction. The man is guilty and still in prison; the paperwork that put him there was not clean. Vale obtained the original file and has held it over you ever since.

Find Cassie Chase, the heiress, Dr. Beverly Steele and Dakota Steele, the private eye. Tonight can begin with an ordinary conversation, though off duty or not, you will notice things.

items.title: Who Was Beside the Decanter
items.content:
You saw Vale drink wine poured from his private decanter. You did not see anyone identifiable interfere with it. Your instincts want something firmer than the nervous faces around you.

When you looked up after the collapse, Dakota Steele, the private investigator, was already beside the decanter. Ask her what she saw there, and what she did next.

items.title: Laboratory Report
items.content:
LABORATORY REPORT
Vincent Vale — 10 October 1986

The residue from the silver compact marked VV (C1) and the wine from Vale’s private decanter and final glass (W1) contain the same batch of stimulant formulation. Medical findings show that the amount he swallowed in the wine was fatal.

The separate dish (D1) contains a different sedative, in a non-lethal amount.

The fabric swab (F1) is consistent with the stimulant found in the compact and wine. The tests cannot show when it reached the fabric or who was wearing it at the time.

These results do not show who added the stimulant to the wine, when it was added, or whether it came from the compact.

items.title: The Price of Keeping Quiet
items.content:
Vale held the file that could end your career. Tonight nobody holds it, and you feel relieved. You do not trust relief, least of all your own.

Somebody else here may have been paid to feel relieved. Dakota Steele, the private investigator, has been very quiet since the collapse. Ask her whether anyone paid her to keep quiet tonight, and what for.

items.title: The Doctor's Explanation
items.content:
Two years ago you fabricated evidence to secure a conviction. Tonight every fact will come from a witness's own mouth or the laboratory's page.

You hold the laboratory report, a copy for every table: hand one to each table now. It says the fatal dose was in Vale's private wine. Find Dr. Beverly Steele, the Harley Street doctor, and ask what she can tell you about the sample in the silver compact marked VV.
items.footnote: IN YOUR ENVELOPE · Item F: 8 laboratory reports, one for each table · SHARED: hand one to every table

items.title: An Old Remedy
items.content:
At a retreat years ago, you put valerian and skullcap in Vale's wine as a small revenge. Tonight you saw Beverly speak privately with Ronnie Reels, but saw no dose or compact change hands.

Ask Ronnie Reels, the filmmaker, whether whatever Beverly gives him has felt any different lately. You know how easily somebody can make a private remedy sound entirely benevolent.

items.title: The Promise on the Label
items.content:
You saw Beverly speaking privately with Ronnie Reels, but not what, if anything, she supplied. You read auras, not futures: you know nothing of who benefits from Vale's death, but nearly every aura here is begging for reassurance.

Labels lie. Your own 'spiritual' herbs were never quite what you called them, and Vale played the same trick on Roxy Riot's protest songs. Ask her what he sold that was never what the label said.

items.title: A Calmer Kind of Wellness
items.content:
You are a hippie healer with your own wine. Years ago, at a retreat, you slipped valerian and skullcap into Vale's wine: a spiritual practice, you called it, and also a small revenge. Thirty years of retreats have taught you who is medicated and who is merely tired.

Tonight you intend to look serene and faintly otherworldly. Gaze into Vincent Vale's aura with a misty look and offer him a playful reading of his future, then find Tina Tanktop, the aerobics guru, Ronnie Reels and Roxie Runway, and compare approaches to keeping people well.

items.title: A Less Comfortable Explanation
items.content:
What you pour tonight is exactly what the label says: chamomile, lemon balm and a little valerian, nothing that needs a prescription. You saw Beverly and Ronnie Reels talking, not a dose being given.

Ask Tina Tanktop, the aerobics instructor, exactly what she saw in Vale before his final drink. You want an observation, not another flattering explanation.

items.title: Always Performing
items.content:
Twenty years in the ring taught you to read a person in seconds, and most of this room is performing. The best performance tonight was Veronica Vane's: just before the music, she was playing hostess at the drinks, handing out glasses right beside Vale's private decanter. It looked like a star working the room. Now you are not so sure.

Ronnie Reels pointed a camera at the whole evening from the east wall. Ask the filmmaker what his position let him see near the private drinks, and who he recognised there.

items.title: The Roles He Offered
items.content:
Vale mocked your acting dreams while keeping you in cheap cereal adverts. You smiled for the work and hated needing it. During the music, you stood at the dance-area edge; guests turning towards the stage blocked your view of the decanter.

Was it the crowd, or the lights? Wanda Wires was at the side lighting position: ask her whether the house lights went out.

items.title: More Than a Wrestling Pose
items.content:
You are a retired wrestler turned cereal-advert star: patient, imposing, and more sensitive about your acting than your size suggests. Vale mocked your screen ambitions and used the humiliation to keep you taking cheap adverts.

Find Larry Loveboat, the lounge singer, and Ricky Blaze, the stuntman and club owner, and talk about life in show business. You would like one conversation tonight that treats you as a professional.

items.title: Outside Your View
items.content:
You stayed near the dance-area edge during the music and could not see the decanter stopper or the faces beside it. What you do know about is Vale's money: he paid you to smile in cheap adverts and thought he had bought the man as well.

People say Ronnie Redhand took Vale's money during the strike. Ask her what it bought from her.

items.title: Where a Copy Might Be
items.content:
Nobody at the toast heard VV-1, but your file says Barry Byte, the ByteCorp salesman, supplied Vale's tapes and kept a copy of each for himself. If he has VV-1, you will learn whether you were sent after a state secret or somebody's private shame.

Ask Barry Byte what is on his VV-1 copy, and whether anything he copied for Vale touched government business.

items.title: The Recording That Never Played
items.content:
You were sent to find out what VV-1 held before it played. It never played: the toast ended first. Whoever holds a copy now holds Vale's leverage. Your file names 'Nev' Neville, a former GCHQ technician who worked on Vale's systems, as the likeliest leak.

Before you go near Nev, find out who else went near Vale's recordings. Ask Vance Vellum what his reception photographs show: a camera notices who stands where.

items.title: A Recording Called VV-1
items.content:
You work in surveillance and keep it understated. Your service has heard that Vale's archive holds a recording labelled VV-1, due to be played at tonight's toast. Nobody knows what is on it. Your orders: find out before it plays, and stop it quietly if it touches state business. If Sir Giles Houghton asks, tell him nothing: he is too well connected in Whitehall.

Find Sir Giles Houghton, Tina 'Tank' Thatcher and Ronnie Redhand. Be pleasant, and give nothing away.

items.title: Not a State Secret
items.content:
VV-1 was never state business. It is the BBC tape of Veronica Vane admitting she signed away half her fees: evidence for the police, which you will give to Inspector Donna Reed rather than Sir Giles.

That leaves 'Nev' Neville, the man your file named as the likeliest leak. Tell him your file was wrong about him, and ask what he was afraid of tonight.

items.title: A Comeback Under Threat
items.content:
You know what it costs to have Vale decide your future. He replaced you with Veronica, then used your sabotage to keep you quiet. Now you want to understand what he intended to do to her career tonight.

Penny Page writes Vale's speeches. Ask her what she was asked to write for the toast, and whether it mentioned you. Those warm words were never his.

items.title: A Pointed Compliment
items.content:
You were the scream queen of VHS horror until Vale decided Veronica's face would sell better and dropped you like a bad rash. You sabotaged his set in revenge, and he has kept that disgrace handy ever since. The role you would most like remembered is still Night of the Crimson Bride.

Find Veronica Vane, Lucien Luxe and Fiona Fringe. Ask Veronica about her new role, charmingly, if a little pointed. Lucien may want your advice.

items.title: The Part You Lost
items.content:
Vale replaced you with Veronica, and you sabotaged his set in revenge. He kept that disgrace available whenever you became inconvenient. You still resent losing the part, but remember who made the decision.

Ask Veronica Vane about her new BBC role. You want to know what a comeback looks like when Vale still has a claim on you.

items.title: Behind the Wellness Label
items.content:
Vale kept your old sabotage handy for years. Whatever he meant for Veronica's comeback, he meant to do it the way he once did it to you. The part you lost looks different now.

Miss Cherry Bomb's brand is all image too, and Vale used to hint that her tonics were not what the label said. Ask her what is really in them, and who supplies it.

items.title: The Fee Argument
items.content:
Your older copy is labelled VV-1, Vale's own label for the tape. In the BBC recording, Vale claims half Veronica's performance fees and her voice admits signing his management agreement. You kept it as insurance for yourself; it was recorded before this gala.

Find Tommy Tech and compare what is on his copy. Two copies may survive even when one powerful owner is gone.

items.title: Connected Business
items.content:
You sell for ByteCorp, and you always have a deal to offer. You supplied Vale with 'digital insurance' tapes and kept a copy of each for yourself. In your world, knowledge is currency and leverage is security.

Find Peter Packard, the technology investor, and Tommy Tech, the computer consultant. Peter Packard is talking up a network that would connect everyone. Ask how it could be used to share stories about people: anything that reaches everyone can carry an embarrassing story too.

items.title: An Insurance Copy
items.content:
You supplied Vale with copies of private recordings and kept an insurance copy of your own. It contains no footage of tonight. Vale, for his part, kept a copy of everything in his digital archive.

Word is that Mandy Modem has been inside that archive. Ask her what she found there, and whether any of it could explain what happened to him tonight.

items.title: Beyond the Recording
items.content:
Your VV-1 copy holds the BBC argument about Veronica's management fees, not pictures of tonight, and keeping it gave you leverage of your own.

You have spent a career selling the idea that a copy proves something. Find Fiona Fringe, who designed Veronica's gown, and ask whether the mark on its hem could have got there innocently, and when.

items.title: The Gossip You Sold
items.content:
You sold Vale's green-room gossip, what his guests said off air, to the tabloids for cash. He knew what you had done, and could make a scandal out of the man who usually sells them.

A Harley Street doctor keeps better secrets than any green room. Ask Dr. Beverly Steele what she was supplying Vale before tonight.

items.title: An Observation Before a Headline
items.content:
Your trade in Vale's green-room gossip was private commerce: the favourite story this year was that Vale had promised his ballerina, Sasha Smirnoff, a slice of his estate.

Somebody paid DJ Spinny T in cash tonight. Ask him who paid him to raise the music and what the instruction said. You know what an unsigned payment is worth, because you have taken one.

items.title: An Eyewitness Worth Hearing
items.content:
There is a much bigger story than green-room gossip now, and it needs a real source rather than your loudest theory.

Ask Brenda Blip what Vale promised to play at the toast and what she heard in the BBC studio. A first-hand account is worth more than an interview you have already written in your head.

items.title: Names Worth Knowing
items.content:
You host a tabloid talk show and thrive on drama. For years you have sold Vale's green-room gossip to the tabloids for cash. He knows, and a host exposed as a leak would make quite a story.

Find Sabrina Sinclair, the tabloid journalist, Brenda Blip, the Radio 1 DJ, and Vance Vellum, the gossip columnist. Interview them, flatteringly, about what Vale has planned for the toast. Gossip, never accusation.

items.title: The Work You Called Neutral
items.content:
You tapped rivals' phones for Vale and built the archive that held the results. You called the work neutral because that made accepting his money easier. The playback was armed after the collapse, with no play command given and no way to cancel it remotely.

Find Mandy Modem and ask what she actually accessed. Tell her what you helped build.

items.title: A Quiet Technical Chat
items.content:
For nearly two years Vale paid you in cash, with no paperwork, to tap rivals' phones and build the recording system his archive runs on. You told yourself it was just engineering. Whenever somebody mentions Vale's system, they are describing something you built.

Find Mandy Modem, the hacker-for-hire, and 'Nev' Neville, and talk shop. A casual professional conversation may tell you how much they already understand about Vale's system.

items.title: The Switch That Was Not Pressed
items.content:
You checked the playback after the collapse: it was armed, but nobody had given the play command. It would only play once Vale gave the word after the toast. The microphone fault could not remotely cancel it. The insecure archive was a separate matter.

Tell Leo Lights what you found, then ask what cue he followed at 19:29 and how it was arranged.

items.title: What You Built
items.content:
You built Vale's recording archive, which could be read without leaving a complete access log. You also built the separate local playback arrangement. Cash work with no paperwork seemed convenient until you started wondering who else had been inside.

Tell 'Nev' Neville how weak the archive's security was and ask why Vale's recordings worry him.

items.title: Managing Publicity
items.content:
You are a showbiz agent who has spent decades controlling access to fame. You once leaked a rival's tape, and Vale threatened to expose you for it.

Find Frankie Faith, the television evangelist, and Lola Lasalle, the fitness-video queen. Talk about managing the press: they both have an image to protect. Keep your own leaked tape out of the pleasantries.

items.title: Your Own Worst Fear
items.content:
The tape you leaked gave Vale something to hold over you. You fear that private disgrace may be what tonight's promised recording was about, but you have not heard the queued item yourself.

Ask Tommy Tech what he copied from Vale's files. Find out whether the story you dread is actually the one he heard.

items.title: A Movement Below
items.content:
You leaked a rival's tape, and Vale threatened to expose you. From the balcony, you saw a hand near Vale's private decanter during the music. You could not identify its owner, and your angle did not show what happened inside it.

Ronnie Reels, the filmmaker, was filming from the east wall; if anyone caught the face, his camera did. Ask him whether it was pointed near the drinks when the music rose.

items.title: The Balcony Angle
items.content:
Your balcony view showed an unidentified hand near the decanter during the music. You could not name the person or see anything added to the wine. Your own leaked tape taught you how much damage an interpretation can do.

Compare your view with Ronnie Reels, the filmmaker. Ask whom he recognised and what the crowd prevented him from seeing.

items.title: The Paid Cue
items.content:
You followed the anonymous instruction in the deep-red envelope: “At the toast cue, raise the music for twenty seconds. No delays.” You did not see who left it. The music rose, then subsided before Vale began his toast.

Ask Leo Lights what happened to the lighting. You were paid for attention, but never told why someone wanted it moved.

items.title: An Anonymous Request
items.content:
You are a former pirate-radio DJ who has never signed a contract in your life. An anonymous deep-red envelope brought you cash and a typed instruction: “At the toast cue, raise the music for twenty seconds. No delays.” You took the job without knowing the sender or the reason.

Find Leo Lights, the gaffer, and his technician Wanda Wires first: tell them to follow your lead and switch off the stage lights when your music rises. The house lights stay on. Nikki Neon wants her songs played, and Scooter, the backstage messenger, knows everybody's business.
items.footnote: IN YOUR ENVELOPE · Item A: deep-red envelope E1 (dummy money and the music slip) · PRIVATE

items.title: Private Cue for the Toast
items.content:
GM TO SPINNY — give privately immediately before the toast. This unrounded record is the operational copy of the Round 0 cue, not a second distraction.

At the GM's discreet cue, begin Died in Your Arms Tonight slightly early and raise it enough to turn attention toward the stage. Leo has been told to follow your lead: he switches off some of the stage lights as the music rises. House lights remain unchanged. Hold the noticeable music cue for about twenty seconds, then fade it cleanly. Let it look like an over-eager show cue, not a blackout.

Vale waits for the cue to subside before beginning the speech, drinks during it and collapses at the agreed dramatic moment. Do not play Comeback Girl: the fictional operator never receives Vale's play command. The physical envelope contains the same twenty-second instruction.

items.title: The Two Instructions
items.content:
Your deep-red envelope paid for twenty seconds of music, with no sender named. You did not see its delivery. Keep it with the typed slip: “At the toast cue, raise the music for twenty seconds. No delays.”

Find Dakota Steele, the private investigator, and compare envelopes and instructions. You want to know whether your anonymous employer bought something besides a musical flourish.

items.title: The Doorway View
items.content:
From your booth you could see Ricky outside the main-room doorway from the start of the music until the alarm. You kept that doorway in view the whole time, and he did not come through it. You could not watch the private decanter at the same time.

Tell Inspector Donna Reed what you saw.

items.title: A Mark on the Hem
items.content:
After the toast you noticed an unfamiliar pale mark caught in the hem of Veronica's gown. You designed it, and used no tailoring chalk on that hem. You cannot tell what the mark is by looking.

Tell Veronica Vane what you noticed. This is her gown, and you would rather she heard about it from its designer.

items.title: A Gown Worth Noticing
items.content:
You design shoulder pads, and you notice what people carry, what they touch and how they move in their clothes. You designed Veronica's gown; for now it is simply your best work on the best possible model. Tonight you are quietly pushing your new shoulder-pad line.

Find Veronica Vane, the comeback soap star, Angie Vixen and Lucien Luxe. Admire how Veronica wears the gown, and see who else might be in the market for shoulder pads.

items.title: Where the Sample Came From
items.content:
You reported the pale mark from Veronica's gown for examination. The sample is labelled F1; it came from the hem you inspected after the toast. You do not yet have the test result.

Tell Inspector Donna Reed where the mark came from and when you noticed it. The detail that troubled you as a designer may matter for a different reason.

items.title: The Gown and the Report
items.content:
You designed Veronica's gown and identified the pale trace in its hem after the toast. The submitted sample, F1, came from that gown. You can say where you found it, but not when it first got there.

Read the laboratory report on your table, then find Inspector Donna Reed and ask what the fabric finding shows about the gown, so the garment is more than an unexplained sample label.
items.footnote: ON YOUR TABLE · The laboratory report, handed to your table by Inspector Donna Reed · SHARED

items.title: The Lights Stayed On
items.content:
You followed Spinny's cue at 19:29. The stage and disco lights changed with the music, while the house lights stayed on. From the lighting board you could not see the private decanter.

Ask DJ Spinny T what musical instruction he followed. You want to know how the cue you operated was arranged.

items.title: The Request Before the Cue
items.content:
Before the toast, Veronica asked you to arrange a twenty-second music rise with stage lights, calling it a surprise for Vince. Spinny was away from his desk. You saw her leave a deep-red envelope there, but did not open it.

At first you thought it was celebrity fuss. After the collapse you feared being blamed for helping. Tell Glenda Gold what you saw. Someone who understands discreet payments may understand why you hesitated.

items.title: Agreeing the Cue
items.content:
You are the lighting gaffer for the evening: practical, alert, always aware of timing. You were asked directly for a twenty-second music rise with the stage and disco lights just before the toast (a surprise for Vince, you were told) and you agreed, because agreeing is the job. The house lights stay on.

Find DJ Spinny T, your technician Wanda Wires, Nikki Neon and Scooter, the backstage messenger. Speak to Spinny first and follow his lead: when his music rises, switch off some of the stage lights and tell Wanda which ones are hers.

items.title: Twenty Seconds Before the Speech
items.content:
You timed the music and coordinated stage-light cue from 19:29 to about 19:29:20. The house lights stayed on. Vale began his toast afterwards, and the collapse brought the alarm at 19:30.

Tell Brenda Blip the timing and ask what Vale had promised would follow the toast. Your cue was only one part of the planned evening.

items.title: The Art of Being Remembered
items.content:
You are a New Romantic pop star, used to attention and to secrecy. Vale recorded you without consent in a compromising backstage scene, and you have been waiting for him to use it. Keep an eye on how differently Vale is served tonight.

Find Angie Vixen, the scream queen, Veronica Vane and Fiona Fringe. Angie was a Vale Meridian star long before you and is still working: ask her advice on building a career that one tape cannot end.

items.title: A Private Vintage
items.content:
Before the toast you noticed Vale drinking from his private decanter while everyone else had champagne. You did not watch it throughout, and cannot say who went near it. Your attention kept drifting to the recordings Vale might use against you.

His archive is still out there. Angie Vixen, whose advice you sought at the reception, has lived with his threat far longer: ask her what Vale kept on her, and how she lived with it.

items.title: Who Owns the Performance?
items.content:
Vale filmed you without consent in a compromising backstage scene. You fear the damage it could do, but you do not know that this is the recording he intended to play tonight.

Penny Page watched Vale pass her words off as his own. Ask her why she has had enough, and tell her why being recorded without a choice makes his control feel personal.

items.title: Beyond a Dramatic Impression
items.content:
Vale's private wine caught your eye, but you did not see it tampered with, and your fear of his backstage footage explains your nerves, not the decanter.

Ask Vance Vellum exactly what his decanter photograph shows and when he took it. A striking image deserves a careful look before anyone builds an accusation around it.

items.title: The Herbal Story
items.content:
You relabel Beverly's stimulant, bottle it in rose-coloured glass and sell it at cosmetics-counter prices no herb could ever justify. Vale held the formulation and supply records that could expose unlicensed medicine behind the brand.

He once joked that Glenda Gold paid him more for silence than you charge for a bottle. Ask Glenda what paying Vale for silence bought her.

items.title: A Promising Label
items.content:
You are a cosmetics queen, and your Cherry Bomb Wellness tonics are not herbal. Their active ingredient is a stimulant Dr. Beverly Steele supplies you privately; you relabel it, bottle it in rose-coloured glass and sell it at cosmetics prices. Vale holds the formulation and supply records.

Find Glenda Gold, the jewellery mogul, Graham Greenwell and Polly Premium. Talk brands and labels, and keep Beverly's ingredient out of it. You and Graham both know what a promising label can do.

items.title: What You Have Been Selling
items.content:
You built a respectable wellness brand by disguising Beverly's stimulant as a herbal product. Vale could expose the arrangement. Now you wonder how many people here believed the label.

Ask Marianne Moonbeam what she actually puts in her preparations. She has spent a lifetime believing in the thing you have been selling, and you would like to know how that feels.

items.title: The Ingredient You Share
items.content:
Beverly supplies the stimulant ingredient. You bottle the diluted finished product in rose-coloured glass and sell it through Cherry Bomb Wellness. Vale kept the records. During launch planning, you compared your supplier reference with Graham's; his proposed remedy uses the same ingredient.

Ask Graham Greenwell what his paperwork says about the connection. This is business knowledge you would both rather had remained private.

items.title: The Clause You Read
items.content:
At the solicitor's appointment, Vincent had you look over family papers. As you remember it, his right to half Veronica's future fees lasted only for his lifetime, but you will need the paperwork to be sure. If that is right, the estate you were counting on is worth far less than anyone imagines.

Ask Sasha Smirnoff whether Vincent promised her part of his estate, and how much.

items.title: What Ends With a Person
items.content:
The paperwork is in front of you now. Clause 7 of Veronica's management agreement reads:

“The Manager shall receive one half of all fees paid to the Artist for her performances, for so long as the Manager lives. On his death this right ends, save for sums already due, which pass to his estate.”

His death has cost you more than anyone: the estate you inherit is poorer without those fees. You have spent a lifetime being the other one; tonight you are the one with the answers.

Tell Veronica Vane what the clause says.

items.title: The Brother Who Arrived Afterwards
items.content:
You are Peter Vale, Vincent's twin brother and a television producer, long in his shadow. Your finances are strained; as his heir, you have always assumed his estate would one day put that right. You arrive at 19:55 after leaving a solicitor's appointment in Cheltenham at 19:30, and nobody told you about the collapse. The taxi driver's note confirms your journey times.

Find Penny Page, who wrote your brother's words tonight, and ask what he meant to say.
items.footnote: IN YOUR ENVELOPE · Item B: taxi-driver journey note · PRIVATE

items.title: Keeping Your Temper
items.content:
You are an ex-stuntman turned nightclub owner, tough and impulsive. Vale funded your nightclub with dirty money, and you forged his signature to keep the loan alive. Your temper has got you into more trouble than it ever got you out of. Tonight you want to avoid another ugly scene.

Find Larry Loveboat, the lounge singer, and Marshall 'Macho' Monroe, and talk about old work. Larry's smooth manner might help you keep your temper.

items.title: Another Man's Bad Temper
items.content:
You were outside during the music and remained there until the alarm. That does not erase the forged loan signature Vale held over you.

Now Rex is getting the treatment you know too well: one bad temper, and the whole room decides he did it. Larry Loveboat saw Rex below the guardrail. Ask Larry when he saw him, and whether he stayed.

items.title: The Signature You Forged
items.content:
You forged Vale's signature on loan paperwork. He could expose you, and your temper made it easy for him to provoke another scene. You went outside and were there during the music.

Find Marshall 'Macho' Monroe and ask how he kept working for a man who mocked his ambitions. You recognise the effort of looking untroubled.

items.title: Beyond the Doorway
items.content:
You stayed outside the main-room doors from the start of the music until the alarm. Larry passed and noticed you, but you would like to know whether somebody saw more than a passing moment.

Ask DJ Spinny T whether he could see the doorway from his booth during the cue.

items.title: Another Planned Humiliation
items.content:
Vale never told you what else he planned to announce tonight, and you would rather ask than assume every recording concerns your humiliation.

Sabrina Sinclair came with a notebook to write up whatever Vale announced. If he kept a tape on a reporter too, she will know how he used them. Ask her whether Vale kept a recording of her.

items.title: Old Music, Old Bargains
items.content:
You were the smiling face of Take Watt; now you are a solo artist, and Vale still owns your old songs and image. When he announced a Take Watt reunion tour with Roxy Riot and Rex as support, you told him you would rather walk away: too volatile, and not your style. You sing ballads; they set things on fire. You do not know who heard that outburst.

Find Johnny 'Jet' Maxwell, Rex 'Razor' Steele and Roxy Riot. Ask Johnny what happened when the hits stopped, and be polite to Rex and Roxy about the tour.

items.title: Built By the Same Man
items.content:
Vale still owns your old songs and your image. When he announced a Take Watt reunion tour with Roxy Riot and Rex as the support act, you told him you would rather walk away. You do not know who heard the outburst.

Vale built Lucien Luxe the way he built you. Ask Lucien what he fears Vale might still release, and whether either of you ever found a way out.

items.title: The Time You Spent in the Lobby
items.content:
You stayed in the lobby signing and talking from about 19:28 until the alarm, relieved to be away from Vale's tour talk.

You still do not know who heard you tell Vale you would rather walk away. Ask Johnny 'Jet' Maxwell how much of the lobby time he saw, and whether your voice carried as far as you fear.

items.title: A Duet Worth Arguing About
items.content:
You are a punk-turned-goth icon, once Vale's most controversial discovery. You never forgave him for turning your protest songs into pop jingles. Now he wants you and Rex as the support act on the Take Watt reunion tour: punk's most dangerous woman, warming up screaming fans for Robbie Rayne's old boy band.

Find Rex 'Razor' Steele, Robbie Rayne and Johnny 'Jet' Maxwell. Ask Rex what he expected from the performance, and Robbie what he thinks of his new support act.

items.title: The Performance Nobody Heard
items.content:
Your early guitar outburst does not explain what Vale intended to play after the toast.

Tommy Tech has been muttering about copies of Vale's files. Ask him whose career the copied BBC conversation threatened. You are beginning to wonder whether the evening's cruellest performance was one the audience never heard.

items.title: The Broken Guitar
items.content:
You broke your guitar around 19:20 after the performance arrangements fell apart: an angry outburst, well before the later music cue. Vale had spent years turning your rebellion into something he could sell.

Roxie Runway, the model, has been jumpy all evening, and you have heard he kept footage of her too. Ask her what Vale did with her public image.

items.title: One Crash, a Later Crackle
items.content:
Your guitar broke in your own outburst around 19:20. The music cue came later. You do not know what caused the brief microphone crackle people heard during that later moment. What still makes you angriest is older: he sold your protest songs as advertising jingles for the very things they attacked.

Ask Peter Packard, the tech investor, when he heard it.

items.title: A Messenger's Small Job
items.content:
Vale personally commissioned Comeback Girl for after the toast and tomorrow's paper; you can stand behind the title and the deadline. You have spent the evening hoping nobody finds his old tape of you offering him money for a story.

Everyone is hunting tapes, and nobody has asked the messenger. Find Scooter and ask what Beverly asked her to carry.

items.title: Tomorrow's Story
items.content:
Vale commissioned a story called Comeback Girl, to follow the toast and appear in tomorrow's paper. You also fear the recording he kept of you bribing him for an earlier story.

Comeback Girl sounds like a comeback story, and the last comeback Vale touched was Johnny 'Jet' Maxwell's punk reunion, which left him in debt. Ask Johnny what recordings or reunion arrangements made him nervous.

items.title: A Headline in Waiting
items.content:
You write for the News of the Screws. Vale told you to bring a notebook for a story called Comeback Girl, for tomorrow's paper, but has not told you what is in it. You once bribed him for stories, and he recorded that conversation.

Find Brenda Blip, the Radio 1 DJ, Chuck Chambers, the talk-show host, and Vance Vellum, the gossip columnist. Find out what they expect Vale to say at the toast, and note anything useful in your notebook.

items.title: The Commission You Heard
items.content:
Vale gave you the title Comeback Girl and told you to report it after the toast for the next morning's paper. You heard that commission directly from him. You did not hear the original BBC studio conversation yourself.

Comeback Girl is a story about a contract, and Sid Scrape faked signatures for Vale. Ask Sid which contracts he forged, and whether Veronica's was one.

items.title: A Small Favour
items.content:
You look like a courier, easily overlooked. In fact you run deliveries for a quiet stimulant network, and Dr. Beverly Steele is one of the people you carry for. Tonight she gave you a sealed silver compact marked VV for Veronica, calling it a formulation sample for Vale's inspection.

Collect the compact from the Game Master and hand it to Veronica Vane in secret, still closed, so that nobody sees. Then find DJ Spinny T, Leo Lights and Nikki Neon.

items.title: The Luxury of Being Forgotten
items.content:
Beverly gave you the silver compact marked VV, sealed, and you carried it to Veronica before the toast. You did not open it, and you never saw its contents go into the wine.

You carried one thing meant for Vale; Cassie Chase stopped another. Tell Cassie about the delivery and ask whether Vale ever received the dish she sent back.

items.title: The Compact You Delivered
items.content:
Beverly asked you to carry a sealed silver compact marked VV before the toast, calling it a formulation sample for Vale's inspection. You delivered it sealed, without opening it.

Ask Dakota Steele, the private investigator, whether the compact she recovered is the one you carried. Do not name who you gave it to yet: you carried it in good faith and want to know what this is about.

items.title: What You Carried
items.content:
Beverly supplied the compact and you delivered it sealed to Veronica. Ask Dakota Steele what happened to the compact after you delivered it, and borrow it from her. You never inspected what was inside it.

Take it to Dr. Beverly Steele, the Harley Street doctor, and ask whether it held an ordinary finished dose or an undiluted sample. You want to understand the favour you carried.

items.title: A Different Public Face
items.content:
You are a Yorkshire union activist, tough and outspoken. You once worked in intelligence as Patricia Thatcher, and documents in that name still exist. You were not sent here officially, but you recognise what Vale has built: a system for gathering information and using it as leverage.

Find Ronnie Redhand, a fellow union organiser, Agent 'Rosemary' and Sir Giles Houghton. Talk about who gathers information on whom, and notice who seems too at ease with it.

items.title: The Name in the Passport
items.content:
Patricia Margaret Thatcher was your former working identity in intelligence. You kept the old passport as a private reminder, in a coat you had not cleared out. You sat on the sofa and later found the pocket unfastened. You did not see it fall. You were not sent here on an operation.

Explain your history to Agent 'Rosemary', one old professional to another, and ask what she was really sent here to do.

items.title: An Old Identity, a Current Concern
items.content:
The old passport was yours, kept from your work as Patricia Margaret Thatcher. It may have slipped from your coat near the sofa, but you cannot prove nobody moved it. You were not here on a mission.

Tell Sir Giles Houghton about your former identity and ask what sensitive material concerned him.

items.title: The Power of Private Recordings
items.content:
You recognise the power of stored private material: the holder can choose when to expose it, while everyone else waits. That pattern was familiar in Vale's dealings, but it does not identify a speaker you never heard.

Ask Nikki Neon what words she overheard and whether she could recognise the people speaking.

items.title: A Promising Remedy
items.content:
You are a pharmaceutical entrepreneur with a sample case full of promises. With Dr. Beverly Steele you are launching a 'herbal' remedy that depends on a stimulant she supplies. You believed it safe, but Vale has started asking about formulations, supply paperwork and Cherry Bomb Wellness.

Find Glenda Gold, Miss Cherry Bomb, the cosmetics queen, and Polly Premium. Pitch your remedy as business with a future in the growing health and fitness market.

items.title: A Familiar Ingredient
items.content:
Your planned herbal energy remedy depends on a stimulant supplied by Beverly. You understand packaging and profits; she understands the chemistry. Calling it natural has helped you avoid awkward questions.

Ask Miss Cherry Bomb whether Vale ever came asking about her formulations. If he was building a file on her, he was building one on you.

items.title: Your Wellness Remedy
items.content:
You planned to sell a “herbal” remedy although you knew it contained Beverly's stimulant. The finished product was to carry a small, diluted dose; an undiluted sample was meant to make many of them, not to be swallowed at once.

Now you wonder what it would have cost to keep Vale quiet. Ask Glenda Gold whether paying him ever made her feel safe.

items.title: A Shared Supplier
items.content:
Your launch paperwork identifies Beverly as the supplier of the stimulant used in your proposed remedy. The finished product was meant to contain a small, measured, diluted dose. During launch planning you and Cherry compared supplier references.

Ask Miss Cherry Bomb what her own paperwork says about the shared supplier. Two sets of documents naming one source is a different problem from one.

items.title: A Friendly Watch
items.content:
You are a private eye: observant, discreet and methodical. You were hired to keep an eye on Cassie Chase. Watch the drinks area and the people moving through it, and keep a clear account of what you personally see.

Find Cassie Chase, the heiress, Dr. Beverly Steele and Inspector Donna Reed. Be friendly and let Cassie talk; watching somebody is easier when they think you are simply interested in them.

items.title: The Person You Recognised
items.content:
From the west pillar, you recognised Veronica at the private decanter during the music. You saw her face and the stopper, but the people between you hid her lower hands. Earlier you had watched Scooter deliver her the compact sealed.

You accepted money for silence. Letting that silence help conceal a killing is another matter. Tell Veronica Vane what you saw, and why you did not say it sooner.

items.title: The Compact Beside the Wine
items.content:
After the collapse, you noticed a silver compact marked VV beside Vale's private decanter (given to you by the GM). It was no longer sealed. You have kept it for examination, rather than treating it as a dropped cosmetic.

Show Inspector Donna Reed where you found it and describe its markings. Your work watching Cassie has led you to something you did not expect.

items.title: The Payment You Accepted
items.content:
Before the music, you saw Scooter hand Veronica a sealed silver compact. After that handover, still before the music, you found money in a deep-red envelope in your coat, with the typed words: “Say nothing about what you saw near the drinks.” You did not see who put it there. You accepted the money as the price of your silence.

Tell Inspector Donna Reed about the payment and its instruction.
items.footnote: IN YOUR ENVELOPE · Item C: deep-red envelope E2 (dummy money and the silence slip) · PRIVATE

items.title: The Price of Keeping the Work
items.content:
From the side lighting position, you saw guests turn towards the stage while the house lights stayed on. People blocked the view towards the decanter; you were watching the lighting, not the room.

You know how invisible the people who keep an evening running can be, and nobody is more invisible than the messenger. Find Scooter and ask what she was asked to carry tonight.

items.title: Credit and Blame
items.content:
You are a backstage lighting technician working under Leo Lights: quiet, practical and observant. Vale persuaded you to sign off an unfinished rehearsal inspection, then kept the paperwork to hold over you. You regret signing it, but it created no dangerous fault tonight, and you would like your judgement respected again.

Find Leo Lights and DJ Spinny T first: when Spinny's music rises, you switch off your share of the stage lights, as Leo directs. Then find Penny Page, the script editor, and Sid Scrape, the old-school punk, and talk about doing Vale's work while somebody else takes the credit, or the blame.

items.title: The Request Behind the Cue
items.content:
You regret signing that unfinished rehearsal inspection for Vale. Tonight's house lights stayed on; you saw Leo operate the stage cue, but did not know who requested it. You were not paid to keep quiet about the drinks.

Ask Leo Lights who asked for the coordinated cue. You want a straight answer about somebody else's decision, after carrying the blame for your own.

items.title: The House Lights Stayed On
items.content:
You stood at the side lighting position and saw Leo operate the stage and disco lights. The house lights stayed on. You did not know who requested the cue. Your old rehearsal sign-off was premature paperwork, not a dangerous fault at this gala.

Ask Marshall 'Macho' Monroe what he could see when the crowd turned towards the stage.

items.title: A Better Introduction
items.content:
You are a Vale Meridian script editor. For years Vale has paid you privately to rewrite his speeches and television introductions, then presented the best lines as his own spontaneous wit. You wrote tonight's toast. Now you want a proper writing credit.

Find Sid Scrape, the old-school punk, and Wanda Wires, the lighting technician. You have all done Vale's work without your names on it: compare notes on who gets the credit and who gets the blame.

items.title: The Words Before the Toast
items.content:
You rewrote Vale's speeches for private payment and let the audience think the wit was his. This week he asked you to draft the toast: warm words congratulating Veronica on her new role. You wrote them without knowing what he meant to follow them with.

Ask Brenda Blip what Vale promised would come after the toast.

items.title: The Name Left Off
items.content:
You accepted money to let Vale present your speechwriting as his own wit. You want a proper writing credit, even if it means admitting you helped maintain his image. You were his writer, not the keeper of his recordings, and you have not seen his private footage.

Office talk says Vale filmed Lucien Luxe backstage without consent. Ask Lucien why Vale's recordings frighten him, and tell him why you want credit for your work.

items.title: What Your Words Introduced
items.content:
You wanted Vale to acknowledge your writing in public, but you will not fill this gap with another polished invention.

You are sure the local recording holds the key to this murder: Vale meant it to follow the very words you wrote for him. Colin Cable checked the playback after the collapse. Ask him what he found, and whether the room ever heard it.

items.title: A Clean Record
items.content:
You are a retired insurance claims assessor, and you know exactly what a claim form is worth. Years ago you passed several of Vale's claims, a 'stolen' camera, a 'flooded' studio and 'lost' jewellery, knowing they were not honest. You have not spoken since, but he keeps everything.

Tonight you intend to look respectable. Find Glenda Gold, Miss Cherry Bomb and Graham Greenwell, and talk about what a guarantee really covers. Brands and labels make promises; somebody always has to read the small print.

items.title: A Careful Witness
items.content:
Years ago Vale put claims through you that you should not have passed. He never mentioned them again, which worries you more than if he had.

Before the toast you saw Lola greet Frankie warmly, and then the two of them slipped away. You did not follow.

Ask Lola Lasalle why she is so careful about press attention. Let her decide how much to tell a woman who spent thirty years reading other people's stories.

items.title: What He Kept
items.content:
Everybody agrees Vale kept a copy of everything. If he kept your claim forms, they could come out now that he is gone, and you would rather know before anyone else does.

Ask Barry Byte, who supplied Vale's tapes, whether Vale's archive held paperwork as well as recordings.

items.title: Hearing It From Me
items.content:
You passed Vale's false claims years ago, and neither of you ever mentioned them again. You had no reason to be near anything of his tonight, and you were not.

Tell Inspector Donna Reed about the claims, and that you never went near his private drinks table. You would rather she heard it from you than found it in his files.

items.title: Q1-01
items.content: Lucien, Vale built us both the same way: the look, the songs, the secrets. If he kept something on me, he kept something on you. What are you afraid he might still release? Did either of us ever find a way out?

items.title: Q1-02
items.content: Dakota, before the toast I carried a sealed silver compact marked VV for Beverly. I never opened it. Is the one you found the same? I'd rather not say who I handed it to until I know what this is about.

items.title: Q1-03
items.content: Ricky, people say you forged Vale's signature on a loan. What did Vale do with it? Did he use you the way he used others?

items.title: Q1-04
items.content: Brenda, I had a hand in the warm words Vale was going to say about Veronica tonight. What did he promise would come after the toast?

items.title: Q1-05
items.content: Veronica, after the toast I noticed a pale mark caught in the hem of your gown. I used no chalk on that hem, and I can't tell what it is by looking. I would rather you heard it from me.

items.title: Q1-06
items.content: Dr Steele, I saw a covered dish carried back to the service hatch where you were standing, and you looked rather worse than Cassie did. Why did it come back?

items.title: Q1-07
items.content: Dr Steele, I hear a great deal about what people take before they go on. Vale seemed unusually sharp tonight, even for him. What were you supplying him before the gala?

items.title: Q1-08
items.content: Lola, you guard your image like a policy. I spent thirty years reading other people's stories. Why are you so careful about press attention?

items.title: Q2-01
items.content: Penny, you write Vale's speeches. What were you asked to write for tonight's toast, and did it mention me?

items.title: Q2-02
items.content: Penny, you wrote Vale's words and watched him take the credit. Why have you had enough? I have my own reasons to hate the way he controlled other people's images.

items.title: Q2-03
items.content: Dr Steele, the silver compact Scooter carried: did it hold a ready-to-take dose, or a sample meant to be diluted?

items.title: Q2-04
items.content: Brenda, I have a copy of the BBC recording from your studio: Vale claiming half of Veronica's fees, and Veronica admitting she signed. Does that match what you heard?

items.title: Q2-05
items.content: Dr Steele, the compact I carried for you has turned up, and I have it with me. Did it hold an ordinary finished dose, or an undiluted sample? I'd like to understand the favour I did you.

items.title: Q2-06
items.content: Lady Helena, I stopped Vale's covered dish because its seal had been disturbed. What did you see of it being taken back?

items.title: Q2-07
items.content: Graham, the silver compact held an undiluted sample of the ingredient in your remedy, not a ready dose. What have you been telling investors the remedy contains?

items.title: Q2-08
items.content: Ricky, I saw you outside the main-room doors during the music. It was only a passing moment, so I can't vouch for the whole time, but I did see you there.

items.title: Q2-09
items.content: Lucien, Vale owned my words; I hear he owned something worse of yours, on film. Why do his recordings frighten you? I'll tell you why I want credit for my own work.

items.title: Q2-10
items.content: Mr Chambers, you know what gets said in Vale's green room. What does it say about me, and about Vale's money?

items.title: Q2-11
items.content: Mr Byte, I understand you kept a copy of the tapes you supplied to Vale. What is on your VV-1 copy, and did anything you copied for him touch government business?

items.title: Q2-12
items.content: Spinny, I hear somebody paid you in cash tonight. Who paid you to raise the music, and what did the instruction say?

items.title: Q2-13
items.content: Fiona, what did you notice about Veronica's gown after the toast? I've found something tonight I can't put a time to, and I suspect you have too.

items.title: Q2-14
items.content: Tommy, I have an older copy of Vale's tape, labelled VV-1: the BBC recording about Veronica's fees. What is on your copy? Let's compare.

items.title: Q2-15
items.content: Inspector Reed, the pale mark I reported came from the hem of Veronica's gown. I noticed it after the toast; the sample is labelled F1. It troubled me as a designer, and it may matter to you.

items.title: Q2-16
items.content: Veronica, I was in the BBC studio when Vale said he took half your fees and you said you had signed. Why did that recording threaten your new BBC role?

items.title: Q2-17
items.content: Sabrina, there's talk of a juicy BBC recording behind Vale's big story. Did you ever hear it, or only his word for it?

items.title: Q2-18
items.content: Cassie, I saw a covered dish being taken back towards the hatch. Whose was it, and why was it withdrawn?

items.title: Q2-19
items.content: Ronnie Redhand, word at the bar is that you took Vale's money during the strike. What did it buy from you?

items.title: Q2-20
items.content: Spinny, could you see the main-room doorway from your booth during the music cue? I was outside it the whole time.

items.title: Q2-21
items.content: Scooter, nobody notices the people who keep an evening running, but I noticed you. What were you asked to carry tonight?

items.title: Q2-22
items.content: Mr Vale, I'm told you have read your brother's papers. What did Veronica's contract say: how much of her earnings could he take, and does that stop now he is dead?

items.title: Q2-23
items.content: Leo, I checked the playback after the collapse: armed, but nobody ever gave the play command. Your lights answered the same twenty seconds. What cue did you follow at 19:29, and how was it arranged?

items.title: Q2-24
items.content: Spinny, I gather you were handed an envelope tonight and did exactly what it said. What were you paid to do, and did you ever find out who wanted it?

items.title: Q2-25
items.content: Marianne, you seem to see more than most. Will you gaze into the auras here tonight and tell me whether any of it threatens me?

items.title: Q2-26
items.content: Mr Byte, you supplied Vale's tapes. Did his archive hold paperwork as well as recordings?

items.title: Q3-02
items.content: Dakota, before the music I saw Veronica slip a deep-red envelope into your coat pocket at the cloakroom. What was in it?

items.title: Q3-03
items.content: Vance, what exactly does your decanter photograph show, and when did you take it?

items.title: Q3-04
items.content: Marianne, what do you actually put in your preparations? You believe in wellness the way I sell it, and I'd like to know how that feels.

items.title: Q3-05
items.content: Inspector Reed, I have read the laboratory report. Does it show who put the stimulant in the wine? I'd like to hear your answer for myself.

items.title: Q3-06
items.content: Fiona, during the music I saw Veronica's profile beside the private decanter, in the gown you designed. What did you notice about that gown?

items.title: Q3-07
items.content: Spinny, the recording Vale meant to play was the BBC exchange about Veronica's fees and her new role. What did your anonymous music instruction pay you to do?

items.title: Q3-08
items.content: Cassie, I carried one thing meant for Vale tonight: a sealed compact, to Veronica. You stopped another. Did Vale ever receive the dish you sent back?

items.title: Q3-09
items.content: Wanda, people say Vale made you sign off a rehearsal before it was finished, then kept the paper. What was that like? Is signing your own name under pressure better than faking someone else's?

items.title: Q3-10
items.content: Inspector Reed, before we talk properly: what do you make of what the laboratory found in the separate dish?

items.title: Q3-11
items.content: Colin, I'm sure the local recording holds the key to this murder. You checked the playback after the collapse: what did you find, and did the room ever hear it?

items.title: Q3-12
items.content: Veronica, I have my brother's management agreement in front of me. Clause 7 says his right to half your fees ends with his death; money already owed stays with the estate. I thought you should hear it from me.

items.title: Q3-13
items.content: Nev, I owe you this: my file was wrong about you. What were you afraid of tonight?

items.title: Q3-14
items.content: Brenda, what did Vale promise to play at the toast, and what did you hear in the BBC studio? I'd rather have a first-hand account than my own theory.

items.title: Q3-15
items.content: Ronnie Reels, during the music I saw Veronica's face as she went to the private decanter, but people hid her hands. How much did your camera position let you see?

items.title: Q3-16
items.content: Mr Lights, just before the toast the music and stage lights rose together, as if on a signal. Who asked you to arrange that cue?

items.title: Q3-17
items.content: Inspector Reed, I have read the laboratory report. What does the fabric finding show about the gown?

items.title: Q3-18
items.content: Veronica, from the west pillar I saw you at the private decanter during the music. I kept quiet for reasons I'm not proud of. I'd like to hear your side.

items.title: Q3-19
items.content: Dr Steele, the laboratory report says the fatal dose was in Vale's private wine. What can you tell me about the sample in the silver compact marked VV?

items.title: Q3-20
items.content: Glenda, before the toast Veronica asked me to arrange the music-and-lights cue, calling it a surprise for Vince, and I saw her leave a deep-red envelope at Spinny's desk. I kept quiet for fear of being blamed. I think you'll understand why.

items.title: Q3-21
items.content: Larry, everyone is deciding Rex did it because of his temper. You saw him below the guardrail: when, and did he stay?

items.title: Q3-22
items.content: Leo, who asked you for the music-and-lights cue? I've carried the blame for my own decisions; I'd like a straight answer about somebody else's.

items.title: Q3-23
items.content: Lady Helena, I understand Vale could have said something about your name, and that you have lived with that a long while. What was it he held? I have reasons of my own for asking.

items.title: Q3-24
items.content: Miss Fringe, you designed Veronica's gown and I gather you found something on it after the toast. What was in the hem, and could it have got there innocently?

items.title: Q3-25
items.content: Mr Reels, you had a camera on this room from the east wall all evening. What did your position let you see near the private drinks, and did you recognise anybody there?

items.title: Q3-26
items.content: Polly, you noticed my greeting with Frankie earlier. May I explain it to you properly?
